utterances.text: Well, given the -- the positions held by the participants in the meeting, one would expect that strategic level decisions are -- are made. I mean, sometimes the -- the distinction with the operational level may be difficult to make, but at least would you expect strategic level decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You say based on the participants at the meeting. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, you have senior officials from the VJ; namely, General Perisic who is the chief of General Staff and General Mrksic who is commander of the special forces corps. You have senior officials of the Republic of Serbia, I mean, President Milosevic, as well as of the MUP Serbia, and you have -- you read them out, and you have the counterparts from the Republika Srpska. So -- I mean, those are the highest political authorities and -- sorry, political and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you have any comments on Karadzic's -- the notes in terms of Karadzic's statements on this page and what their relevance are to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the bottom of the page you can see that he reiterates the six strategic goals. It may be a -- a typo or something -- I mean, not a typo but an error in taking notes. But both strategic goals 5 and 6 have been inverted. But otherwise they -- the goals as set or the strategic objectives as set by Karadzic are the same ones as he mentioned in May 1992 -- 12 May 1992 at the 16th Assembly Session and as have also been reiterated in the various directives of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 60 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this page we see additional notes of comments by Jovica Stanisic and also then later on by Tomo Kovac. Do you have any comments on what these notes show?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Jovica Stanisic's comments or those attributed to him show that he is discussing the -- the -- the -- a special group for -- for night-time distance operations, which would consist of 100 to 120 men. I mean, we have to see this in context of other documents, but at face value one would expect that he is talking about making a group of the MUP Serbia available with the characteristics as he describes there, and he also talks about setting up a Joint Staff from -- consisting of representatives of MUP Serbia as well as from VRS units. I mean, Visegrad and Sinica are brigades of VRS units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What does this show about Jovica Stanisic's level of situational awareness of events that are going on in Bosnia at both the operational and tactical level?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it shows at least for this part that he discussing operational/tactical matters. I mean, he -- he seems -- he's familiar or he seems to be familiar with that part of the Drina valley, yeah, which shows an understanding of tactical -- of the tactical and operational situation in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just going down to Tomo Kovac, do you have any different comments than what -- those you have just made with respect to Mr. Stanisic or any more detailed one?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's the same level of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Prior to this date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- could I ask -- is everything about Mr. Kovac, is that on this page or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It may continue onto the next page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because before we say that it is the same detail, could we have a look at the next page? It's unclear to me whether this continues to represent what Mr. Kovac said. Could I ask you, Mr. Theunens, when you said the same level of detail what did you have in mind? And could we go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I can answer without the page. What I had in mind was the level of detail in relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But I'd like to have the previous page. There we are. Zoom in on the lower part in the Stanisic and the Kovac observations. Yes. You said that what is written down here shows a similar level of detail compared to what Mr. Stanisic said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my answer referred to the nature of -- of forces that have to be -- or that seem to be under discussion to be engaged to conduct operations. Kovac does not go into geographic details but he talks about -- I mean, he gives detailed information on the size of a unit that can be made available including the deadline within which that can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, but how does that show any awareness of the situation on the grounds? If I say, I'll spend 500 euros on a charity, what does that say about my knowledge about the charity? It says something about that I'm willing to spend 500 euros. So, therefore, Mr. Stanisic refers to brigades and positions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and in that context offers or at least says how much men he would be willing to make available. So I was a bit puzzled by your observation that it was a similar level of awareness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I apologise for the misunderstanding, Your Honours. What I meant by the level of detail was, as I explained in my subsequent answer, the level of detail in relation to the -- the size of a unit and the deadline within which that could be made available. Kovac obviously does not make any comments on the tactical situation in the area. One would assume that, I mean, when is he talking about engaging a unit that he also understands where this will be and if he gives a deadline. The location where that unit is to be used obviously impacts on a deadline because there is a duration of transport. So -- but I do agree with you he does not give any -- in his answer or in his comments he doesn't give any detailed -- any comments -- he doesn't comment at all on the geographic or tactical situation in the region discussed by Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm again looking at your answer in relation to Stanisic and then in relation to Kovac. And you said about Stanisic: "He seems to be familiar with the situation in that part of the Drina valley here which shows as understanding of tactical and operational understanding in that area." And then you were asked about Kovac. You said: "No, it's the same heavily of detail." In your first answer to Stanisic, you clearly referred to a -- I would say knowledge of the tactical situation, not just about numbers to be made available. So, therefore, it was somewhat confusing, now having heard your further explanation. Mr. Weber you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, how did these comments relate in terms of the context of this meeting and the strategic goals that we saw Mr. -- or Dr. Karadzic discuss earlier? At least according to the notes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what I have to say because, I mean, it's clear in the document. We are talking about the situation in the Drina valley where Mr. Karadzic gives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I earlier observed that if the story is about the Drina valley and then when you ask the witness does that correlate in any way with the strategic goals that unless there is any reason to -- despite mentioning Drina valley, it nevertheless should be understood as Neretva, unless we have such an exceptional situation, the Chamber is available to recognise that Drina valley and Drina valley are the same words and therefore refer to the same strategic goals unless explained otherwise. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your report, you've included a significant number of intelligence reports from Zdravko Tolimir. Is Mr. Stanisic including amongst the addressees on these intelligence reports or a good number of them?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is Your Honours. And this is discussed on page 341 of Part 2 of the report, and I mean the reference -- the inclusion can be seen in the addressee list of the references under footnote 1245.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is the reason that individuals would be included on an addressee list of an intelligence report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows that there is a recognised need to know for these individuals to obtain or to receive that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, if Mr. Theunens would not have answered the question, I would have said you address something to someone because you want him to know about what is in that document. Now, have you ever heard of any other reasons to address -- well, there may be a more specific one, to act on it or something like that. But even if you want to know whether someone has to act upon something, you'd need to know the content. I mean, let's not ask for the obvious. Let's focus on what really matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'm going to move onto another topic right now. I'd like to talk to you about the topic of logistics and General Mladic's involvement in this area. Could you please generally tell us, first, the nature of General Mladic's involvement in logistics.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, summarising the documents I have discussed in my report, General Mladic issues orders on how logistic support can be requested from the VJ, and he also issues orders on the redistribution of certain weapons systems. For example, when we are talking about the modified air-bombs and the equipment that is required to use them. He also issues several, I would say, numerous requests to his counterpart in the VJ, General Perisic, to obtain logistic supply - mainly ammunition and weapons - for the VRS in order to conduct operations between, say, May 1992, and where Perisic is concerned, of course, and this is after August 1993 and November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P3029, English page 435 and B/C/S page 432.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'm going to be calling up page 219 of Part 2 of your report. On this page of the report, you include an excerpt of General Mladic's statements during the 50th RS Assembly Session in April 1995. What does his comments specifically show about the condition or his involvement in VRS logistics?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the comment doesn't really reflect General Mladic's involvement as I have explained in my previous answer, but it shows his awareness of the logistic requirements, in particular, for what ammunition is concerned for the VJ -- for the VRS, and he -- I mean, he also provides detailed information on the consumption of ammunition by the VRS during combat operations. And, as I mentioned, he gives a very detailed breakdown as to the provenance of that ammunition. For the different types of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution now go to 65 ter 8869.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move on, is this uncommon for a commander at his level to be briefed by his staff and subordinate units on precise percentages to have this kind of knowledge? I mean, I do understand that - and I take it, unless you believe otherwise - that he did not had all these percentages ready from the top of his head but that someone provided to him, so he most likely has asked for it or at least it was offered to him, is that uncommon if you address the audience in the situation where he was in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think there are different components in your question. It's obviously not uncommon that the commander of the Main Staff or the chief of General Staff receives detailed briefings on the logistics situation of his army, i.e., what is consumed and what is available and where does it come from. However, on -- this entry refers to what General Mladic himself is stating to the members of the RS Assembly Session. So obviously he has not made a calculations himself. He is sharing the information he has obtained from his assistant commander for logistics. I mean, it could be debated whether the members of the parliament need such detailed information. But in any event General Mladic, who had obtained this information, considered it necessary to share it with the assembly members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, necessary or not, he did it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the document that's up before you -- actually, the exhibit that -- the upload in front of you contains a series of documents related to different types of materiel. The first document on this is 23 January 1994, Main Staff logistic sector notification from Major-General Djordje Djukic. Does this document show specifically where the mortar shells -- the supply of mortar shells are coming from? At least according to this document.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, in paragraph 3 mention is made about the supply of mortar shells, i.e., rounds by a factory in Valjevo, in Serbia. And this has been approved by, I mean, by the chief of general -- by the General Staff of the VJ. Yeah, that's what the document states. It's difficult to find out what happens after; I mean, how these mortar rounds are to be brought to the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have the next page. These documents are not necessarily linked in that fashion, so as not to confuse the matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a document from Pretis.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What does this document indicate in terms of General Mladic's involvement?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document states that the deployment of -- of ... guns, I mean, two types of gun for operational support that are being manufactured in Belgrade, that this deployment is to be approved by General Mladic. So it shows co-operation between not only the VJ and the VRS but also their respective ammunitions or weapons factories and production facilities with the approval, obviously, of the -- of the VJ and the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to have similar questions on the next couple of documents. I don't know if Mr. Ivetic is okay with me tendering this document all of these documents at this time. There's a total of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- five documents in this upload.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's Pretis --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we do need to have questions because, in particular, I'm reading this as being Pretis in Vogosca, which I think is different than the company that was on the first page. I must admit that I had not seen this one on the list, and so I'd not paid particular attention to this 65 ter number to be familiar with the remaining five documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: These documents are not necessarily -- they're each independent but being offered for the same purpose. And the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is that there was communication between the higher level army authorities with the production -- the companies producing, in this case, ammunition. Is it all about ammunition or is it about the others, Mr. Weber? Because here you specifically have drawn our attention to the mortar shells produced by Pretis Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, well, I must say - one second, please. Yes, I think it's all Pretis Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually the first page indicates the mortar shells are from Krusik Valjevo in item 3, and I believe that's also then referring to 120-millimetre LTF shells from Krusik again in the later document. Then I believe in the last document there's reference to different types of shells and FAB 100s and 250s, so it's -- for what you're saying, but it shows different examples of the types of munitions being provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Munitions provided by the various producers and the communication with the higher level of the VRS --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- command. Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just trying to take a glance at each of the documents, Your Honour. If you could just bear with me. One more document, I believe, is in the bunch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you allow me, the one in front of us talks about guns. So it's ammunition and guns or other equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the specific portion Mr. Weber addressed was about ammunition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we're introducing for the purposes of ammunition, then I guess I don't have an objection to the remainder coming in although I'd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They're a group -- they're a group 65 ter numbers, so I guess there should be one number, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's be very practical. We'll decide on admission. And, Mr. Ivetic, if there's any matter which comes to your mind, well, let's say within the next two hours, having looked at it a bit more in detail, then you can revisit -- revisit the matter, and it will not be held against you, that you did not oppose admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 8869 receives P3073, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3073 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 14607.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, this is a Main Staff sector for the rear technical department document dated 11 July 1995 from Miroslav Crvecic [phoen]. What does this document relate to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document addressed to the Pretis factory instructs the latter to issue materiel. Based on what I see, this materiel consists mainly of ammunition, mortar ammunition, as well as tank ammunition to the SRK. And it's then further specified that this is needed for operations in the south-western part of the Sarajevo theatre of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And continuing on, does it indicate any other areas of operations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on what I can see on the screen. I'm sorry, it's also mentions the north-western part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. I am a bit puzzled by the ... whether that's -- it seems to be envelope information, the Sarajevo automobile factory, what that has to do. It seems ... could we have a better look at the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It shouldn't -- Your Honours, if you allow me, it shouldn't be part of the original because the original is a telex which starts at the left top corner the heading, i.e., the originator. The reference to TAS -- I mean, it cannot be part of the original document unless it is recycled paper. But in my view, it's not part of the message that is sent by the Main Staff to Pretis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it is part of the original as presented to us. So, therefore, I see it looks as if it is a -- either a letterhead or an envelope top down, where apparently something is addressed to the Main Staff of the VRS. Pretis is mentioned. Mr. Weber, any -- any explanation for --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Offhand, I don't have an explanation. I could either look into it and report back to the Chamber or -- we don't intend to rely on that information. If you'd like me to see if -- we could redact that top part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it raises some concerns about how you put your documents together. That's -- we do understand that it is not what you seek the Chamber to rely upon. At the same time, it raises some concerns about the precision with which these documents are prepared. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P3074, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's okay with you, and I'm going to try to ... Your Honour, if it's okay if I further discuss with Mr. Ivetic, there's some other logistics-related documents to see if we can [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber -- the Chamber never opposes any discussions you have with Mr. Ivetic which would be in the interest of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I now want to return for a moment to an exchange, a conversation you had with Judge Orie yesterday in relation to the recorded conversation of General Mladic in which he stated that those older than 10 and younger than 75 ... in Sibenik would come to harm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE SAID TO YOU
utterances.text: "Yes. But if -- are these instructions already? You say he is not going to consider. What makes you believe that he is not going to reconsider?" In your response, you highlighted the important difference between two people having a conversation and a military commander having a conversation with his subordinate. My question to you is: In a situation where a military commander issues an order and subsequently reconsiders the decision and decides he does not want the original order implemented, what, if anything, is he obliged to do with respect to the original order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I'll have to object because it improperly categorises the material that was before the Chamber and that was being discussed as being an order. I believe my recollection of Your Honours' question to the witness was that this was in reference to something that if something happened, then, and that -- that no order had been issued yet as to the contingency having transpired. So to categorise this as an original order, I think misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, what I remember, it was a conversation where it was said: If this and this happens, then we would -- of that kind. And otherwise we get the text before us and first explore whether this is considered to be an order or a conditional order, as you put it yesterday. Perhaps we should have the text --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's fine. Without expressing a view on whether or not General Mladic said is probably considered an order or not, I can ask my question in -- in theoretical terms in a situation in which a commander issues an order. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As long as it is clear that if it would not apply to the situation you refer to, then, of course, it may hang somewhere in the air without any link to -- because you introduced the matter clearly in the context of the questions I put to the witness yesterday, which was a very specific context. And now to say: I'll do it in a very general way, then, of course, the relevance for what we looked at yesterday may be lost. I leave it in your hands, Mr. Weber, whether you would either go back to the text we saw yesterday or that you put questions of a very general nature to the witness. But then you should ask yourself to what extent that would assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, just going back to my question, in a situation where a commander issues an order and subsequently reconsiders the decision and decides he does not want the original order implemented, what, if anything, is he obliged to do with respect to the original order?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he has to make clear that it's not valid anymore. And that it's replaced by another order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could just, please, have one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 17293A -- or, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, on the screen before you, can you tell us, do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours. It's a 1983 textbook or regulation of the JNA for command and control, which I have quoted extensively in my report. Part 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can we please go to page 23 in both versions. I'm not sure if we need it enlarged. If we could have the bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please summarise for us what this particular section deals with.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It deals with -- I mean, as the text says, it is obviously predicting as part of the command process. That is, obviously in order to plan operations, as a part of command and control, you do not only have to be familiar with the current situation of your own units, enemy units, any factor that can influence your operations, but you also have to be able to make -- yeah, predictions, i.e., to be able to foresee how these factors can develop. For your own forces, you may be able to foresee how ammunition consumption will develop based on the nature of the operations they will conduct. Obviously you will have a weather forecast, if the weather may have implications for your operations. And as for the enemy, you have the intelligence organ who, on the basis of their understanding of -- of enemy doctrine and the nature of the terrain and so on, try to make predictions as to how the enemy is going to act in the -- in -- in the time that is of relevance for the conduct of your own operations, including how the enemy will respond to your operations. And all these factors together will be used then in order to prepare plans aimed at implementing the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can we now move to e-court page 24 in both versions, next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to the paragraph immediately above the section entitled: "Decision-making." This paragraph relates to the importance of commanders considering the possibility of different scenarios as well as different solutions to those scenarios. Can you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could scroll up on the screen, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can you read this paragraph to your yourself, and when you're done, could you please explain this concept to us in just lay -- lay terms.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Summarising this, Your Honours, it means that while surprise in -- sorry. While surprising the enemy is a requirement for successful operations, the commander himself does not like to be surprised in relation to potential future developments. So when predicting the various developments, each staff section in their own area, they will have to do scenario-building and at least include the best -- the worse-case scenario because then at least even if the situation develops in a way that was not exactly predicted, the impact of surprise should be reduced because the unit -- I mean, the command and the forces have prepared for the worse-case scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does a commander have an obligation to supplement or change his orders in response to an evolving situation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it all depends of the task that has been set. If the evolution of the situation does not have any impact on the way how the unit can accomplish the task, then there is no need to amend the order. If, however, the changes do impact on the ability of the unit to achieve the task, then, of course, the orders have to be amended, in order to limit or eliminate the impact of the changes on the desired end state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can a commander give an order that becomes effective upon the occurrence of a future event -- upon the occurrence of a future event, such as if the enemy forces launch an attack on a village, artillery fire should commence on an enemy command centre, for example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could I ask you. You said would you ask questions about a very general theoretical level. It's -- in my ears I hear resounding the situation we discussed yesterday. Is that your purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going come back to it. If you would like me to do now, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you whether that is that the purpose of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going back to that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So this is all relevant. It's not that theoretical. Then I'd like to ask a few questions about what happened yesterday. Yesterday we looked at this telephone conversation between Mr. Mladic and Lieutenant-Colonel Milisav. Could you tell us exactly who Lieutenant-Colonel Milosav was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the assignment this Lieutenant-Colonel Milisav at that stage. You know, if I would be given the opportunity to again review the documents and to do a search --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first have a look at the document itself, which is P1959, I think. Could we have a look at it. Page 3. What is it that makes it takes so much time? There we are for the B/C/S. English page 3. Yes, there we are. I think we still would need to move in the B/C/S perhaps also to page 3. I'm not quite sure about that. Mr. Theunens, on the top of that page is said that Ratko Mladic said: "In Zadar, they are blocked. They're asking for negotiations ... we will stop firing, to see if they will permit a normal evacuation ..." And then Milosav answers: "Would you also have us as part of that?" And then Mr. Mladic says: "As we are looking at you also as part of that, to get you out as well." Is it your understanding that Mr. -- Lieutenant-Colonel Milosav is belonging to units that would need to be safely evacuated from the Zadar region? Is that your understanding of what's written here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my understanding, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, those units that are seeking to be evacuated safely, in your view, would that be the same units as that would embark on the destruction of Zadar if negotiations would be unsuccessful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you allow me I will give a two-fold answer. First, from a methodological point of view, I rarely draw conclusions on one single document because that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to draw any conclusions. I'm just asking how you understand this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you can put them in the context of other documents, you, of course, have an opportunity to do so. But my question was whether, reading this text, you think that those troops to be evacuated safely, whether those are the ones you would expect that would be tasked with the destruction of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if this Lieutenant-Colonel Milosav is in Zadar and if he is in the JNA artillery centre in Zadar, where, for example, there were Orkan multiple-barrel rocket-launchers, and I think it was the only installation in the JNA where these weapons were available, then, of course, he would be in a position to use these weapons against targets identified by General Mladic. This is just on the face value, knowing what Zadar was and what was there. So the answer would you yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If, then yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, looking at the language, "if they do not agree, then we will impact on the distribution of Zadar," purely from the point of view of the text, do you consider this to be an instruction given to Lieutenant-Colonel Milosav, or action to be taken by whatever unit under the command and control of Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean, it's very difficult to -- it's clearly not an order as we have seen before. But at least it -- it reflects Mladic's state of mind as well as it could be interpreted as the commanders intent; i.e., what is the general view of Mladic in relation to the situation in Zadar? How he will translate that general view of his general objective in orders to his -- his subordinates is another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but - if I may interrupt you at this moment - many of the previous questions put to you by Mr. Weber were about what would you need if you do not further persist on an order? Now, if you say to a lieutenant-colonel, who is not necessarily the -- commanding the units that would have to destroy Zadar, if you just say, We will, and if you had in mind that another unit would be tasked with that, if it ever comes to it, because only if the negotiations were not successful, wouldn't it be totally unclear now who would have been aware of what to do? And, in this respect, if you are informed about the intention a potential -- an intention in case something would happen, would you then have to inform that person that either the negotiations were not successful and that, therefore, the intention had been withdrawn or just that you changed your mind? I'm rather confused about the questions that were put to you in this same context --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which seems not to directly apply to the present situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm asking a question to Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean, an order has to be clear and has to say when the action has to be conducted, I mean, in clear terms. Obviously an "if" is not enough --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also should it not include who is addressed by the order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. But I do believe that what General Mladic says is important because, again, as I mentioned earlier or in the days before in your answer, this is not a conversation between two people we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'm not asking questions whether you consider it important. I'm not in any way -- in my questions have put the importance of the matter on the table.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you some additional questions which were triggered by the questions that were put to you as questions of a general kind by Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Yes, Your Honours. It is not an order to Milosav to start shelling Zadar but it -- I'm repeating myself. It shows General Mladic sees -- as the commander how he sees the situation there. And you know we could turn it around. Mladic doesn't have to mention that. Mladic doesn't have to say, We will bomb Zadar if they don't do that. He is a military commander. He is having, I think, a conversation about the situation with -- with a subordinate commander or with a subordinate officer - we don't know what position this Lieutenant-Colonel Milosav has - but at least it shows to the subordinate officer the mindset and the commander's intent of General Mladic in relation to Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear to me. Mr. Weber, you wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- address something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So it doesn't get too confusing, this wasn't the section of the conversation I was referring to in my questions. It was the last page so -- just so that's clear on the record. But can I go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, returning to this section --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we take a break first --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because we are at that point. Yes, then I was the more confused, if it did not even relate in any way to this part, because looking forward, the ifs, and telling that an order was not valid anymore -- well, I hope -- I apologise for not fully understanding it. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just say something so that the Chamber can think about over the break and maybe avoid this confusion. The Prosecution isn't dealing with any of this evidence to establish that General Mladic gave an order, legal or otherwise, regarding Zadar. We're introducing this evidence because of what it speaks to with respect to his mens rea and his general disposition towards civilians in the conduct of war. That's simply it, Your Honour. And if Mr. Weber is indulged with a few more questions, all of this will become very clear after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, if is about the mindset, then of course it is a matter totally different. But the questions were mainly about looking forward and in -- the questions were not primarily about the mindset. I at least understood them not to be. We take a break. We first ask Mr. Theunens to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber. You exclusively wanted to address the matter of the 301 and the 306, and the -- the Sibenik people coming to harm. Is that the portion you wanted? Yes. And no one getting out of Dalmatia except children under the age of 10. Yes. Okay. It's all about mindset. We take a break, and we resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to come into the courtroom, Mr. Weber, it certainly would have assisted, if, when referring to yesterday's conversation, if you would have given a clear reference as -- in terms of the source of that, which might have -- which might have avoided further confusion. Perhaps I should have asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to call up -- I'm returning to 65 ter 17293A. If I could please have page 31 in e-court in the English. And I'm afraid I do not have the B/C/S. I'm not sure if it's part of the uploaded excerpts. We will look into this; and, if it's not, we will correspond the appropriate B/C/S section. I would just note for the record that, at least of now, it can be found in 65 ter 17293, page 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, before looking at the section before you, I just want to return to what General Mladic said to his subordinate, Lieutenant-Colonel Milosav, that all people between the ages of 10 and 75 may come to harm. Apart from whether or not General Mladic intended this as a specific order, apart from whether or not he may have considered or withdrawn what he said to Milosav, do you have an opinion regarding what the impact of a commander talking about the possibility of committing war crimes with a subordinate has on the functioning of a military organisation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will give a -- a theoretical answer irrespective of the individuals involved by referring to the 1988 regulations on the implementations of the laws of war by the SFRY armed forces. That is, that the subordinate cannot implement an order that would amount to crimes. And so in this case, the subordinate should have made it clear to his commander that if, indeed, he was to implement the task of -- of not allowing anyone between -- or sorry, committing harm to the people between 10 and 75, then he should have made his commander aware of the fact that this would amount to a crime and that he would not be able to implement that order. However, in this context, I mean, considering the personality of General Mladic and the -- I would call it charisma even -- even if I haven't used that expression in my report. But the degree of not just de jure but also de facto authority he has because of his personality and his command style, and in the overall context as we are seeing at that time in -- in -- in Croatia and later on Bosnia-Herzegovina, it may well be that subordinates were less inclined to -- to confront General Mladic with -- with that observation, i.e., that it would amount to a crime and perhaps would have implemented the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I understood the question to be slightly -- to be a different one. What effect that would have on the subordinates rather than how the subordinates would respond to that, and if I look at the -- that such -- that -- I think if I would not be a specialist, I would think that it would give a very bad example. That has got nothing to do with expertise on matters. If you behave in a way which -- or if you talk about things in a way which are not consistent with the regulations, the valid regulations, then that might be understood by others that there's no need to do that and gives a bad example. That is, I think, a layman would easily say. Now, you as an expert, would you agree with that or would an expert think about it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean, obviously we would agree with that. But I mean, you also have to look at the whole context. I'm not sure whether I included it in this report, but there is an ultimatum by General Kadijevic, I believe, of the 1st October 1991, that -- where he clearly states that for each JNA facility that is being damaged or harmed, or JNA personnel being damaged or harmed, we're thinking here of the context of the blockade that was mounted by -- blockades that were mounted by the Croats, that he -- the JNA will retaliate against Croatian towns. There is such a -- a -- an ultimatum by General Kadijevic. So, I mean, in theory, obviously one doesn't have to be an expert to agree that it gives a very bad example in it. But the practical context is such that even the most senior levels were considering this option of retaliating against civilian targets to respond to the Croatian blockade of JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can I now draw your attention to the screen before you and, in particular, the second paragraph on the top of the page which states: "The function of a senior officer requires certain traits that are connected with that function. It is very important that in everyday work an officer acts in conformity with socialist social norms and norms of military conduct, and as an officer in command, he has to adapt his method of work to a military environment." Is this passage a reminder of the importance of avoiding the type of thing you've just described?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it is. And it can be summarised as leadership by example.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution is going to tender this -- selected excerpts from this once we verify the presence of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How many pages is it that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's okay with you, I will -- we've reviewed it for the ones that we feel are necessary, it is a greatly reduced amount of a very large document but it still might be a certain amount -- 42 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber -- 42 pages. That's an answer to my question. We'll marked for identification pending verification of the B/C/S translation. And we may also further consider relevance and -- and if you would -- you said you have done that, the Chamber wouldn't mind if you would do it again so to be perfectly sure and to see whether that changes anything. I have no opinion about it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Mr. Registrar, the number under which it would be MFI'd, would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P3075, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I would just like to clarify my previous answer concerning the Kadijevic ultimatum. This is footnote 411 in Part 1 of the report. It's put there on page 125. And I think shows there the mindset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of Mr. Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And -- and senior leadership in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Before we continue, the Chamber has considered whether it -- first of all, Mr. Theunens, you are scheduled for next week. Would you be available next week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it cause you any problems, for example, to leave on -- to be excused on Friday rather than on Thursday because we are usually not sitting on Wednesday? Would that cause you any problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would not, Your Honours. But it would be appreciated if the ICTY can contact my employer now because they expect me back on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meaning still be in court Thursday morning and leaving on Thursday afternoon. Is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But given the flight schedule, I would leave on Friday then and be back in Lebanon on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Friday would be at what time approximately that you're -- the flight schedule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, it's -- from Brussels it's at 11 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 11.00 in the morning, yes, that's clear. The reason why I'm raising it -- but there's nothing apart from that you'd like your employer to be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not that things would go wrong, where you -- perhaps things may always go wrong if you're wrong if you're not there but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if there's not a specific urgency in your return, apart from that you'd like to be back as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And it is nice to know in advance because I have some practical issues just to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood. Because as I said before, the Judges have -- well, used their Wednesday for appointments assuming that we would not be sitting. Now, Mr. Ivetic, you have -- the witness was scheduled for eight hours of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it was seven, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seven. Which would mean that that's a fair chance even if we would not sit on Wednesday that we'd -- nevertheless, we would be able to conclude by Thursday at the end of the morning session. The Chamber would very much like the parties to see whether we could achieve that. That is, to conclude the cross-examination but also re-examination by Thursday. A day having three and a half effective hours of examination usually would mean cross-examination to be concluded preferably at the end of Tuesday's session. On the basis of what we now discussed, the Chamber sees no reason yet, at this moment, to change next week's schedule, that is, to sit on Wednesday instead of Friday. Mr. Theunens, the expectation is there's a fair chance that you would be excused on Thursday anyhow. If anything changes, then we would inform you as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready, you may start your cross-examination. Mr. Theunens, you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hello, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take up approximately where you left off in the direct examination with the incidents at the Zadar barracks, the JNA troops that were barricaded therein, and the conversation between Lieutenant-Colonel Milosav and General Mladic as we have discussed. First of all, did your review of material lead you to determine how long the JNA forces at the barracks in question had been surrounded and blockaded by enemy Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the purpose of this report, I did not analyse the activities of the Croatian forces, including the duration of -- of -- of -- of blockade of JNA barracks and installations in Croatia. So I'm not able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just intervene for a second. Mr. Stojanovic, I appreciate that you're typing urgent matters, but you could do it at another table so that we do not also hear you typing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours will note that I tried to use the technology available to limit the distance between myself and the microphone but unfortunately it's still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not a matter of distance. I take it that it's a matter of resonance rather than -- so, therefore, changing microphones would not likely result in any positive way. Either you change from desk or refrain from typing. That's the solution, I think. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, did you have occasion in the review of the material in relation to the situation surrounding the Zadar barracks to confirm that the forces located therein, the JNA forces therein, had already suffered casualties in the way of deaths of their members as a result of the activities of the surrounding enemy Croatian troops or forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe I've answered the questions -- the question. I have not analysed the situation of the JNA barracks in Croatia and -- and I mean, the blockade by Croatian forces. I have general knowledge of that, and I understand that there were casualties, but I have no specific information as to -- for the situation in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have information whether the blockade was complete or partial, were they completely surrounded by enemy forces, were they partially surrounded by enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I don't have specific information for Zadar. What I know about Zadar I have mentioned during the questions by Your Honours and the Prosecution. That is that I know there was a blockade and I know that there was the -- that the JNA had the artillery training centre in -- in Zadar, which, if I'm not mistaken, was under the command of then Colonel Perisic and there were modern artillery weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether that particular barracks was one of the ones which had utilities, water and food supplies, cut off from the outside?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- before we continue, is there any issue between the parties that, if you're surrounded by enemy troops, that you'd fight your way out, if need be? Or is the issue about the language used about: We'll embark on the destruction of Zadar. I mean, fighting your way out is something -- well, at least linguistically different from destruction of Zadar. I gained the impression that it was that language, if we're talking about mindset, rather than whether if you failed to positively negotiate, that you would do whatever you think would be militarily necessary. So therefore I'm wondering whether we are -- on what track we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we're on the same track, Your Honour. I'm about to talk about the language that was used and what can be drawn from that with these foundational questions of the expert to set up what would be a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then I think that could have been done more quickly, but I leave it to you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, if I may ask you to exercise your military knowledge, your military experience, and the expertise that you claim to have on military matters to ask you to comment upon a situation. If we are to assume that a friendly military force is surrounded, if we are to assume a friendly military force is cut off from supplies of food, water, and utilities, and, indeed, suffering casualties, would it be a situation where you would consider that a friendly military commander might attempt to try to boost the morale of those so blockaded, and, indeed, promise things that he has no intention of undertaking so as to keep the soldiers so blockaded from giving up or despairing that they are not -- that they are alone in the fight? Is that something that you would expect?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I first need to correct you. I have not made any claims about any expertise I might have, yes or no. I mean, you know by now that this is a matter that is in the hands of Trial Chamber. And concerning the boosting of morale and so on, you know, making abstraction from the military, if you make promises to somebody who is in a difficult situation and you don't fulfil them, I would say from a psychological point of view, without being a psychologist, it makes it even worse for you. From a military point of view, there would have been other ways to boost morale instead of saying that, you know, we're going to destroy the city because how the are the people going to be feel better by having more destruction around them. He could have considered, well, you know, we're negotiating with the Croats, we'll allow food in or they will allow food in. We can fly in food. I mean drop it from helicopters or whatever. I think there would have been more constructive ways to boost morale in this context than to make a promise or -- not a promise, but to threaten to destroy a city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, to the extent you intended to draw the Chamber's attention through the witness that there may be other explanations as for the language used, you have done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may focus on another part of your answer, sir, and ask you, do you consider yourself to be a military expert?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will repeat myself. It's in the -- it's the Trial Chamber who decides whether I or colleagues who appear in the same position are considered experts or not and whether their reports are accepted, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can return to another matter that you dealt with today, we had a set of documents dealing with the Krusik Valjevo factory and the Pretis Vogosca factory --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And by the way, Your Honours, I have reviewed those documents and I do not have an additional objection, so we may proceed to enter them into evidence. That was 65 ter number 8869 according to my notes and it therefore -- I've lost the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were admitted into evidence but you had an opportunity to revisit them [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's now on the record that you do not intend to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record this is P3073.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Fluegge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to that Pretis factory, which according to the documentation was to be receiving and indeed did receive some parts that had been intended for the Krusik factory, did your review of materials indicate that the Pretis factory, that the confrontation line ran through the middle of the Pretis factory in Vogosca such that the Armija BiH had control over one part of the factory, whereas the VRS had control over another part of the factory?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not able to confirm that, but I don't think that that had any impact on the -- on -- the point I tried to -- to demonstrate in my report, i.e., that there is collaboration or cooperation between arms and ammunition factories under Bosnian Serb control and such facilities in FRY and that this collaboration occurs on the instructions and/or with the agreement of the Main Staffs of the respective armies, i.e., the VRS and the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're doing two things. First to see whether e-court is functioning or not functioning again, but the other eye was looking at the clock, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have a better vantage point than I do from here so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- I'm at your disposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that we should adjourn for the day. Mr. Theunens, we'd like to see you back on Monday morning, at 9.30 in the morning. At this moment, I wouldn't know whether it's in this same courtroom. Let me just check. It is in this same courtroom, II. And I give you the same instructions as I did before, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony or communicate in any other way about it. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume, Monday, the 9th of December, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 9th day of December, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.
